suggested_introduction: Good governance, a cornerstone of modern public administration, denotes the manner in which public institutions conduct public affairs, manage resources and guarantee the rights of citizens. It is anchored in the principles of legitimacy, accountability, transparency, participation, rule of law and effectiveness, as articulated by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and scholars such as Osborne & Gaebler (1992). In the Indian context, the concept gained policy prominence post‑1990s, culminating in the National Governance Index and the establishment of the Good Governance Committee (2005).
core_dimensions: 1. Legitimacy & Rule of Law: Emphasis on constitutional supremacy, judicial oversight and protection of civil liberties (Dahl, 1989).
2. Accountability & Transparency: Mechanisms like the Right to Information Act (2005), Lokayukta institutions and social audits (Kumar, 2014).
3. Participation & Inclusiveness: Decentralisation through Panchayati Raj, e‑governance portals (e‑Seva), and citizen charters (World Bank, 2008).
4. Effectiveness & Responsiveness: Performance‑based budgeting, Public Service Delivery Reforms (PSDR) and the National e‑Governance Plan (NeGP).
5. Equity & Sustainability: Pro‑poor policies, gender‑sensitive budgeting and Sustainable Development Goals integration.
key_thinkers_and_models: Samuel P. Huntington – Political Order and Change
David Osborne & Ted Gaebler – Reinventing Government
India’s ‘Three Pillars’ Model: Transparency, Accountability, Participation (Committee on Good Governance, 2005)
critical_evaluation: While India’s legislative and institutional reforms have expanded the governance architecture, implementation gaps persist. The RTI Act, though transformative, suffers from bureaucratic resistance and delayed disclosures. Decentralised bodies often lack fiscal autonomy, curtailing effectiveness. Moreover, digital divide issues undermine e‑governance inclusivity. Critics argue that the ‘good governance’ discourse sometimes masks neo‑liberal agenda, prioritising efficiency over social justice. Hence, a balanced appraisal must weigh procedural gains against substantive outcomes, especially for marginalised groups.
suggested_conclusion: Good governance in India represents an evolving paradigm that intertwines constitutional values with contemporary administrative innovations. By consolidating accountability, participation and effectiveness through robust legal frameworks and participatory institutions, the nation moves towards inclusive development. However, sustained political will, capacity building and vigilant civil society engagement are indispensable to translate the normative ideals of good governance into tangible public welfare.
